title: Beyond Uniformity: Regularizing Implicit Neural Representations through a Lipschitz Lens
claim: A total regularity budget derived from task properties can be split across network components non-uniformly, instead of evenly, to balance smoothness and expressiveness.
layout: Center network diagram flanked by input and output meshes, with budget bars below
description: A color-coded MLP sits in the center, with four hidden layers in orange, purple, green and blue. They are labeled φ1(W1) to φ4(W4), and white input and output nodes bracket them. A lung mesh sits on each side. On the left, the mesh shows points x1 and x2 with green and purple arrows. On the right, the mesh shows the displaced points x1+fθ(x1) and x2+fθ(x2). Below the network, a boxed formula reads K=Lip(fθ) ≤ ∏ ki, under the label 'Total budget'. Two horizontal stacked bars follow, with the same colors as the layers. The 'Uniform allocation' bar has four equal segments k1 to k4. The 'Non-uniform allocation' bar has segments of very different widths, with k1 largest and k4 smallest. On the lower right, a formula defines ki = Lip(φi)Lip(Wi). The eye goes first to the colorful network, then down to the bars.
caption: Bridging the gap between theory and practice in Lipschitz regularization. While Lipschitz continuity offers a principled form of implicit regularization, selecting and distributing the budget K remains non-trivial. We propose a novel, data-driven approach to derive K from interpretable, signalor domain-speciﬁc properties, such as tissue compressibility in deformable registration, and strategically distribute this budget across layers. This methodology allows for a better balance of smoothness and expressiveness compared to uniform allocation strategies.
abstract: Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) have shown great promise in solving inverse problems, but their lack of inherent regularization often leads to a trade-off between expressiveness and smoothness. While Lipschitz continuity presents a principled form of implicit regularization, it is often applied as a rigid, uniform 1-Lipschitz constraint, limiting its potential in inverse problems. In this work, we reframe Lipschitz regularization as a flexible *Lipschitz budget framework*. We propose a method to first derive a principled, task-specific total budget $K$, then proceed to distribute this budget *non-uniformly* across all network components, including linear weights, activations, and embeddings. Across extensive experiments on deformable registration and image inpainting, we show that non-uniform allocation strategies provide a measure to balance regularization and expressiveness within the specified global budget. Our *Lipschitz lens* introduces an alternative, interpretable perspective to Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) and Fourier analysis frameworks in INRs, offering practitioners actionable principles for improving network architecture and performance. Code and experimental results are available at: [https://lipschitz-inrs.github.io](https://lipschitz-inrs.github.io).
